chapter: Family band and learning to play
title: Hearing Frank O'Bannon from the alley of the white theater
summary: Segregated theaters, listening to O'Bannon in the alley, and their first meeting at a party.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But he started me -- like he started me off in playing one of these parties that I told you that Miss Frost arranged for us, you know, the lady that was affiliated with the colleges, a saxophone player -- they had like four theaters that had live music with like six or seven-piece bands in them, in the white theaters and I used to go in the back of the alley and listen to him because he had a beautiful tone on alto. His name was Frank O'Bannon. We -- it was segregated. I couldn't pay to go in, you know, we couldn't go to the theaters. We had to have a theater on our own.
They didn't even have the whites in the balcony, that kind of thing?
No, they didn't even have that in Sherman.

Later on, they did. But then, they didn't even have that. But they had a big alley and I'd just go back there and I would listen to them because they would play sometimes like maybe 15, 20 minutes, maybe sometimes a half an hour, then they would play sometime for the pictures. This was before talkies.
But one night -- I knew who he was -- and one night, at one of the parties, he came up to me, he says, "Gee, man," he says, "you sure can play a lot of hokum."

I said, "Oh, yeah? Thank you." He says, "I'm Frank O'Bannon." I says, "I know. I love you. I'm listening to you." He says, "Where did you hear me play?" So I says, "Well, you played the Ginn Theater." He says, "Sure." But he knew I hadn't been in the Ginn Theater. I said, "Well, look, I heard you in the alley." I says, "I was standing back there," and I says, "your sound is very beautiful." I says, "There's a lot of things I need to learn." He says, "I'll tell you what." He says, "I can't play jazz," he said, "but I can read." I said, "I know you can. You're in that theater, you got to be able to read." So he says, "I can teach you that. That ain't no problem." So he says, "Can you teach me jazz?" That's a hard thing, you know. So I said, "Yeah."
